records.name_note: The catalog lands this species as Butter Beans, not Lima Bean. NC State Extension's dedicated Phaseolus lunatus page renders an alphabetized Common Name(s) list of four separate entries — Butter Beans, Java Bean, Lima Bean, Sieva Bean — so its first entry is Butter Beans and Lima Bean is third; RHS's dedicated page for the same species (plant 105458) leads with 'butter bean' beneath its RHS Plant Profile label and files 'Lima bean' fourth in its Other common names field, which reads 'Burma bean, duffin bean, Hibbert bean, Lima bean, Lima kidney bean, Rangoon bean, Sieva bean, sugar bean'. Both dedicated pages therefore lead with the butter-bean form. NC State's own Description prose does use 'Lima Beans' throughout ('Lima Beans are an annual or perennial, flowering plant, in the bean family, producing edible beans.'), so Lima Bean is recorded here as the widely used alternative. Distinct from Phaseolus vulgaris, landed in this catalog as Green Beans, whose own NC State page carries a separate eight-entry name list (Bean, Beans, Bush Bean, Green Bean, Green Beans, Pole Bean, Snap Bean, String Bean).
records.toxicity_detail: Per NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox's dedicated Phaseolus lunatus page, the plant carries the banner "This plant has high severity poison characteristics." and its Poisonous to Humans block rates Poison Severity High (a human-scoped rating, not a cat/dog-specific one). The Poison Symptoms field states: "Toxic, may be fatal if eaten raw. The raw mature seed is poisonous. The toxic principle is hydrocyanic acid and this is destroyed by thoroughly cooking the seed." The Poison Toxic Principle is hydrocyanic acid. The Poison Part field lists both Roots and Seeds (not seeds alone). The Causes Contact Dermatitis field is set to No. The Plant Type field co-lists Edible and Poisonous among its six values (Annual, Edible, Poisonous, Shrub, Vegetable, Vine). The Edibility field gives the preparation instructions: "Immature seed can be cooked and used like peas in soups, stews. Mature seed should be soaked for 12 hours and thoroughly cooked before being eaten." The page credits thorough cooking alone with destroying the toxin; it does not say the twelve-hour soak does, so neither condition may be dropped from a preparation instruction. No admissible source scopes this toxicity to cats or dogs; RHS's dedicated Phaseolus lunatus page has no toxicity field.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: NC State's Poison block for Phaseolus lunatus has no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tags, and its Poison Severity/Symptoms fields sit under a 'Poisonous to Humans:' heading with no animal named; RHS's dedicated Phaseolus lunatus page (plant 105458) carries no toxicity field, so there is no cat/dog-specific toxicity evidence to confirm or deny.

soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field shows the closed Neutral (6.0-8.0) band, but per the ceiling-check rule the 8.0 ceiling must be verified against RHS's pH field, and RHS's dedicated Phaseolus lunatus page (plant 105458) carries no pH field, so the ceiling could not be confirmed and is omitted.

RHS's dedicated Phaseolus lunatus page (plant 105458) was located but carries only names and botanical details, with no care, pH, position or toxicity fields; no MBG PlantFinder, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD or UGA page dedicated to Phaseolus lunatus was located, so every care value rests on the NC State page.

common_name researched as 'Lima Bean'; landed as 'Butter Beans'. The audit FLAGGED the researched value because neither dedicated page leads with it: NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list puts Butter Beans first and Lima Bean third, and RHS leads with 'butter bean' and files 'Lima bean' in its Other common names field. 'Butter Beans' is NC State's verbatim first list item and matches the catalog's plural style for the sibling Phaseolus vulgaris (Green Beans). No collision with an already-landed common_name. Lima Bean is recorded in name_note.

Four quotes on this record were <title> metadata or joined runs and were replaced with rendered text: the page-title parenthetical standing in for the Common Name(s) list (twice, for common_name and scientific_name_accepted), a comma-joined 'Good Drainage, Moist' where the page stacks the two values, and a seven-value Plant Type list whose seventh value, 'Woody Plant', is the first two words of the next label, 'Woody Plant Leaf Characteristics:'. RHS phaseolus-lunatus page also carries no size data: searched both 'Max Height'/'Max Spread' and 'Ultimate height' (0 hits each).

Searched 'Attracts' on the NC State lunatus page (0 hits) and 'Attracts', 'pollinator', 'Wildlife', 'bee', 'butterfl', 'hummingbird' on the RHS page (0 hits on all pollinator-specific terms; the one 'Wildlife' hit on RHS was an unrelated nav-menu link, not plant data).

is_edible is TRUE but conditional on cooking, not a bare edible claim: NC State's Phaseolus lunatus page states the plant "has high severity poison characteristics," with Poison Symptoms "Toxic, may be fatal if eaten raw. The raw mature seed is poisonous. The toxic principle is hydrocyanic acid and this is destroyed by thoroughly cooking the seed," Poison Toxic Principle 'hydrocyanic acid', Causes Contact Dermatitis 'No', and Poison Part 'Roots' and 'Seeds'. RHS's genus-level text on the same page corroborates edibility generally (Phaseolus 'grown as crop plants for their edible seeds, including ... lima beans') but adds no toxicity detail of its own.

NC State's Edibility field gives the preparation in full: 'Immature seed can be cooked and used like peas in soups, stews. Mature seed should be soaked for 12 hours and thoroughly cooked before being eaten.' Its Plant Type field lists the species as both Edible and Poisonous (noted at landing, verified against the cached copy).

The phaseolus-vulgaris NC State page was read as instructed but describes a different species (common/snap/pole bean, not butter bean/lima bean) and none of its data -- including its own separate poison entry, its 'Fruit Width' figure, or its climbing-method/wildlife-food-source notes -- was used for any field on this Phaseolus lunatus record.
Cultivar-specific sizing was not an issue here since no size figures of any kind were found on either page for this species.

records.name_note: Naming is settled for this species; the confusion is with other genera, not with a sibling Pastinaca. NC State Extension's dedicated Pastinaca sativa page carries an alphabetized four-entry Common Name(s) list — Parsnip, Parsnips, Wild Parsnip, Wild Parsnips — whose first entry is Parsnip, so Wild Parsnip is another name for this same taxon rather than a separate species; RHS lists 'Wild Parsnip' among this species' own Other common names too. RHS's dedicated page renders 'parsnip' as its subtitle beneath the RHS Plant Profile label, and its Other common names field reads "heart's eye, madnep, moronen y moch, queen weed, Wild Parsnip" — parsnip is not in that field, which confirms it as the lead name. NC State's structured module is headed 'Pastinaca sativa is often confused with:' and lists 'Conium maculatum' and 'Heracleum maximum' as two separate entries — neither a sibling Pastinaca. Conium maculatum, already in this catalog as Poison Hemlock, carries entirely different common names on its own NC State page (Deadly Hemlock, Poison Fool's Parsley, Poison Hemlock, Poison Parsley, Spotted Parsley), and Heracleum maximum's own NC State page carries Cow Parsnip among its six names, so the two look-alikes NC State records are poison hemlock and cow parsnip. No admissible source was found stating that parsnip foliage is confused with carrot foliage, so that widely repeated claim is not carried here.
records.toxicity_detail: Parsnip is the safety-critical record in this batch, and its hazard is phototoxic sap rather than ingestion. NC State Extension's dedicated Pastinaca sativa page carries the banner "This plant has medium severity poison characteristics." and its Landscape Problems field renders five stacked values: Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Weedy. Its Plant Type field co-lists four traits: Cool Season Vegetable, Edible, Poisonous, Vegetable. Inside the page's "Poisonous to Humans:" block — a human-scoped heading, separate from the cat and dog presence-flags in the Problems field above it — Poison Severity is Medium, the Poison Toxic Principle is Furanocoumarin, Causes Contact Dermatitis is Yes, and the Poison Symptoms field reads, with no closing period on the page: "Causes skin to become light sensitive, leading to severe burns and blisters. Wear protective equipment when dealing with this plant". The Poison Part field lists all six parts: Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. NC State's Description adds a species-specific handling warning — "All parts of this plant contain furocoumarins which can make skin sensitive to light causing burns so be sure to wear gloves, long sleeves and long pants when dealing with it." — and its Insects, Diseases, and Other Plant Problems line ends "Poisonous and causes severe dermatitis." RHS's dedicated page renders the same hazard under the label "Potentially harmful" in two lines: "Harmful to skin with sunlight. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" and "Pets (dogs): Harmful to skin with sunlight - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers". The two sources disagree on pet scope — NC State tags both cats and dogs, RHS scopes its pet warning to dogs alone — and toxic_to_pets is true on either. Clemson HGIC adds: "Some people may develop a rash from contact with juice from the foliage when working with the plants in direct sunlight, so wear gloves to prevent contact during harvest." Edibility is limited to the first-year taproot: "The fleshy sweet taproot from first-year plants is edible, either raw or baked, boiled, pureed, roasted, fried, grilled, or steamed. It can be used in soups and stews." Identification matters here: NC State's structured module records that Pastinaca sativa is often confused with Conium maculatum (poison hemlock, rated high severity on its own NC State page) and Heracleum maximum (cow parsnip).
unknowns: No admissible source was found stating that Parsnip foliage is confused with carrot foliage; only NC State's structured module (Conium maculatum, Heracleum maximum) was usable for name_note.

NC State's Light field for Pastinaca sativa reads 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day),' which is NC State's generic site-wide Full Sun category legend text rather than species-specific prose, so direct_sun_hours_max was left null per the scope-discipline rule.

RHS's Position field also lists 'Partial shade' for this species, but that value was excluded from outdoor_sun_exposure because NC State's structured Light field states only Full sun unconditionally; the conflict is noted rather than merged.

soil_ph_min/max taken from RHS's species-page Cultivation sentence 'The ideal soil pH is 6.5-7'; consistent with RHS's structured pH field (Acid or Neutral), which carries no alkaline band. records.toxicity_detail: Admissible sources disagree about this plant, and the disagreement is the point. RHS's dedicated Parthenocissus tricuspidata page renders, under the label "Potentially harmful": "Harmful if eaten; skin irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" and "Pets: Harmful if eaten; skin irritant - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers". That RHS pet line names no animal, so it cannot set toxic_to_pets under this catalog's cats-and-dogs rule, and toxic_to_pets stays null. NC State Extension's dedicated page for the same species points the other way, listing "Edible fruit" alongside "Wildlife Food Source" in its Play Value field and carrying an '#edible fruits' tag. Because one admissible source calls the fruit edible and another calls the plant harmful if eaten, is_edible is left null rather than shipped as a bare true. RHS's skin-irritant and glove/protective-equipment handling warning stands on its own and is reproduced above in the source's words. No admissible source publishes a poison-part list, a symptom list or a severity rating for this species.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null even though toxicity_detail is populated. RHS's dedicated Parthenocissus tricuspidata page — cited four times elsewhere in this record — does carry a Potentially harmful block reading 'Harmful if eaten; skin irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling' and 'Pets: Harmful if eaten; skin irritant - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers'. That last line is an unscoped 'Pets:' line naming neither cats nor dogs, which under this catalog's rule supports neither true nor false, so the field stays null while the hazard itself is carried in toxicity_detail. NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden and Clemson HGIC publish no poison-part list, symptom list or severity rating for this species. UGA's CAES poisonous-plants factsheet (publication C-957) lists toxicity for the related Parthenocissus quinquefolia (Virginia Creeper), not for P. tricuspidata, so that entry cannot be borrowed for this species per the no-genus-bleed rule.

is_houseplant is false: every admissible source treats Parthenocissus tricuspidata strictly as a hardy outdoor woody climbing vine (NC State Plant Type Perennial/Vine and USDA Zones 4a-8b, Clemson 4-9, RHS Habit Climbing and hardiness rating H5); none addresses indoor or houseplant use, and none frames it as one.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH tags for this species are the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' and 'Alkaline (>8.0)' bands plus 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)', and RHS's pH field likewise lists Acid, Alkaline, and Neutral with no numeric bound, so per the open-band rule no ceiling or floor can be set.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, and the growing/dormant day-interval fields left null: no admissible source frames watering for this in-ground vine as a dry-down target or a day interval. There is also a disclosed tension in the admissible moisture evidence: Missouri Botanical Garden's structured field reads 'Water: Dry to medium' and its Culture text says the vine is 'Easily grown in average, dry to medium, well-drained soils' with Drought/Dry Soil tolerance (leaning toward a drier reading), while NC State's Soil Drainage tags pair 'Good Drainage' with 'Moist' and RHS lists 'Moist but well-drained' (both read as moderate under the stated rule). soil_drainage was set to moderate on the NC State + RHS agreement, with MoBot's drier framing noted here rather than overriding it.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: the only hour figures found ('6 or more hours', '2-6 hours') are part of NC State's site-wide Light category legend text attached to its Full sun/Partial Shade tags for this species, not species-specific prose, so per the rule against using that legend they were not used.

outdoor_sun_exposure includes full_shade based on RHS's structured Position field ('Full shade, Full sun, Partial shade') and RHS's Cultivation text recommending 'partial shade or full shade' for best autumn color, even though NC State's structured Light field for this species lists only Full sun and Partial Shade (mapped to full_sun/part_shade) with no full_shade tag. part_sun was not added since no admissible source's structured field for this species uses that category.

chill_damage_f left null: the only numeric cold figure on an admissible page is NC State's survival statement 'The plant is cold hardy to about 15 degrees F.', which is a hardiness limit, not a damage-onset temperature, and RHS's H5 (-15 to -10 C) is likewise a survival band read off a site-wide hardiness legend, so neither was used. fertilize_interval_days/active_months/strength, humidity_need/humidity_pct fields, day_f/night_f temperature fields and light_fc fields are also null: no admissible source addresses a fertilizing schedule or dilution strength, ambient humidity range, day/night temperature range or foot-candle light levels for this species; all admissible sources treat it purely as a hardy outdoor landscape vine.

name_note left null: NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list for this species (Boston Ivy, Grape Ivy, Japanese Creeper, Japanese Ivy, alphabetized, first entry Boston Ivy), its separate dedicated single-common-name page headed Boston Ivy, Missouri Botanical Garden ('Common Name: Boston ivy'), RHS (subtitle 'Boston ivy') and Clemson HGIC all agree the lead common name is Boston ivy, so there is no split to disclose.

Species scope confirmed on a dedicated single-species page: NC State's structured module states this taxon 'is often confused with: Parthenocissus quinquefolia', and this record deliberately covers only P. tricuspidata (three-lobed leaves, adhesive disc tendrils) without pulling in Parthenocissus quinquefolia (five leaflets) or Hedera helix (a true ivy, unrelated per NC State) facts.

RHS's genus-level Cultivation paragraph ('For the best autumn colour, site in partial shade or full shade. It thrives in any fertile, well-drained soil') and MoBot's Culture paragraph were treated as species-page prose (not shared genus boilerplate) since both appear on P. tricuspidata's own species page, not a genus page.

is_edible left null. NC State's dedicated page supports true — its Play Value field renders 'Edible fruit' then 'Wildlife Food Source', and its tag row carries '#edible fruits' — but RHS's dedicated page for the same taxon states 'Harmful if eaten; skin irritant.' under its Potentially harmful label. Two admissible sources genuinely disagree about whether this plant's fruit may be eaten, so the field is left null and both readings are carried in toxicity_detail rather than one being shipped as a bare true.

mature_height_in_min/max and mature_spread_in_min/max are not carried on this record. NC State's Plant Type field lists this species as a Vine, its Climbing Method field reads Tendrils, and its Description says the plant 'climbs by short tendrils branched with terminal sucker-like adhesive discs'; under the pipeline's climber rule a climber takes no size at all, all four fields null and disclosed, whatever figures the page publishes, because a published height for a climber is the distance it travels along its support rather than the plant's own stature. The figures left unused are NC State's Dimensions block (Height 30 ft 0 in - 60 ft 0 in, Width 5 ft 0 in - 10 ft 0 in) and RHS's open-ended Max Height 'Higher than 12 metres' and Max Spread 'wider than 8 metres', which would give no usable bound in any case.

Two citations were repaired at landing without any value changing: the common_name quote 'Boston Ivy - Parthenocissus tricuspidata' was <title> metadata from the dedicated common-name page, replaced with the species page's rendered four-item Common Name(s) list; and the bare one-word RHS quote 'Correct' was relabelled as the Botanical Details Name Status row and paired with the RHS page-title citation that names the taxon.

records.name_note: Admissible sources disagree on which common name leads for this exact taxon's own dedicated page. NC State's alphabetized Common Name(s) list renders three entries — "Mugho Pine", then "Mugo Pine", then "Swiss Mountain Pine". RHS's dedicated Pinus mugo page instead renders "dwarf mountain pine" as its lead subtitle, listing "drooping cone pine, dwarf pine, mountain pine, Swiss mountain pine" as other common names. MoBot's dedicated page carries a bare "Common Name: mugo pine" line (distinct from its longer, non-quotable Common Names popup list). "Mugo Pine" was selected as common_name because it is MoBot's single Common Name field value and also appears in NC State's list; RHS's differing lead name is disclosed here rather than adopted. Distinct from Pinus strobus (Eastern White Pine) and Pinus taeda (Loblolly Pine) already in this catalog.
records.toxicity_detail: No admissible source reports toxicity to cats, dogs, or any other animal for Pinus mugo. The only edibility-related fact found is NC State's Uses (Ethnobotany) statement that the needles are used to make tea in Bulgaria (a food use, not fruit-based, and regionally specific), alongside medicinal and turpentine-oil uses; no toxicity or handling warning accompanies this.
unknowns: is_houseplant is false: all structured data treats Pinus mugo as an outdoor woody shrub or tree (NC State Plant Type Perennial/Shrub/Tree and USDA Zones 2a-7b, MoBot zones 2 to 7, RHS hardiness H7); no admissible source frames it as a houseplant.
toxic_to_pets: no admissible source reports toxicity to cats, dogs, or any other animal for this species, so the field is left null instead of guessed.

chill_damage_f / cool_rest_note: no admissible source states a specific chill-damage onset temperature; only hardiness-zone ratings (USDA 2a-7b on NC State, 2 to 7 on MoBot, RHS H7) are given, and the task rules exclude zone/hardiness ratings from this field.
day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max: no admissible source gives day/night temperature ranges or humidity requirements for this outdoor conifer.

light_fc_min, light_fc_good, direct_sun_hours_max: no source gives foot-candle figures or species-specific direct-sun-hour prose. NC State's Light field text, 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)', is the site-wide light-category legend, not species-specific prose, so it was not used to set direct_sun_hours_max.

soil_ph_min/max: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0), and Alkaline (>8.0) together, and RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral'; because both open-ended bands are present on both sources, no numeric ceiling or floor can be set.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: MoBot's structured field reads 'Water: Medium', which is mid-scale and per the task rules cannot support keep_moist; no other admissible source gives a watering statement, and as an in-ground shrub/tree no source frames watering by dry-down depth or day interval, so these are left null.
fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength: no admissible source addresses fertilizing this species.

soil_base: set to garden_bed because the species form recorded here is a 20-25 ft shrub/tree that NC State's Landscape Location field places in ground settings (Naturalized Area, Slope/Bank, Woodland) and that MoBot's Uses section places in 'rock gardens, foundations and other small areas around the home'. NC State does also list Container, Patio and Walkways in the same field and tags the plant #container plant, but its own description attaches that use to the dwarf cultivars ('The dwarf varieties can be used in multiple ways including foundations, walkways, containers, patios, and edges of ponds'), not to the species form.

Most Pinus mugo sold in the trade are dwarf cultivar selections rather than the species form; NC State and MoBot both note dwarf/compact cultivars are common in commerce while the species itself can reach the larger mature-size figures reported here, and ungrafted seedlings can outgrow the dwarf habit expected of named cultivars.

The UF/IFAS EDIS publication on Pinus mugo (ENH-626/ST467) that appeared in search results returned HTTP 410 Gone on the live domains (edis.ifas.ufl.edu and ask.ifas.ufl.edu) and could not be verified as still published, so it was not used as a citation source.

A third quote was the page <title> including its ' | North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox' suffix, replaced with the rendered Common Name(s) list. The two single-value Soil Drainage citations were merged into one quoting the field's two stacked values. The bare one-word RHS quote 'Correct' was relabelled as the Botanical Details Name Status row, paired with the RHS H1 citation that names the taxon.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the lead common name for this exact species. NC State Extension's dedicated Cotinus coggygria page carries an alphabetized Common Name(s) list ('Common Smoketree', 'Smokebush', 'Smoketree'); its first entry is 'Common Smoketree', which is not claimed here to be a ranked or designated primary, only the first item of an alphabetized list. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder page for this species displays a Common Name field reading 'smoketree', with no 'Common' qualifier (a 15-name 'Common Names' overlay hangs off that field; it lives only inside an onmouseover attribute and is not quoted here). RHS's dedicated species page renders its subtitle as 'smoke tree' (two words), also with no 'Common' qualifier. All three are dedicated single-species pages for Cotinus coggygria; only the NC State page's lead name was used for common_name per the tie-break rule (first item of a dedicated page's list). This catalog's first Cotinus; distinct from the native American smoketree Cotinus obovatus, which is not in this catalog.
records.toxicity_detail: The only toxicity/handling evidence found on admissible sources is a human-scoped sap-contact warning, not a cat/dog poisoning profile. NC State Extension's Insects, Diseases, and Other Plant Problems section states: "This plant is in the same family as poison ivy and contact with the resinous sap may cause contact dermatitis, especially to those sensitive to poison ivy." NC State's structured Problems field separately lists "Contact Dermatitis" as the sole value. No poison part list, symptom list, or cat/dog-specific hazard was found on any admissible source for this species.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: the only toxicity content found (NC State's contact-dermatitis warning and its 'Contact Dermatitis' Problems tag) is a human sap-contact hazard tied to the Anacardiaceae/poison-ivy family resemblance; no admissible source names cats or dogs, so per the rules this cannot support toxic_to_pets=true.

is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type field for this species reads Perennial, Shrub, Tree, its USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field gives 4a-8b, RHS rates hardiness H5 and its Dimensions are on a ten-to-fifteen-foot scale. No admissible source frames this species as a houseplant.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' text is the site-wide light-category legend, not species-specific prose, so it was not used for this field (though it was used to support the outdoor_sun_exposure value itself).

outdoor_sun_exposure excludes part_shade: RHS's structured Position field lists 'Full sun, Partial shade,' but NC State's Light field and MoBot's Sun field both show Full sun only; per the majority-structured-field rule, the RHS-only 'Partial shade' value was left out.

soil_drainage left null: NC State's Soil Drainage field ('Good Drainage', 'Moist') and RHS's Moisture field ('Moist but well-drained or Well-drained') point toward moderate drainage, but Missouri Botanical Garden's Culture text says 'Tolerates a wide range of soils except wet, poorly-drained ones' and 'Sharp drainage is essential,' pointing toward fast drainage instead. This is a genuine cross-source disagreement, so the field was left null.

soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State's Soil pH field lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0), and Neutral (6.0-8.0) bands, i.e. no stated ceiling or floor; RHS's pH field likewise lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' as all acceptable, so per the rule checking a Neutral-band ceiling against RHS, no ceiling or floor can be set.

water_regime left null: the only structured water field found is Missouri Botanical Garden's 'Water: Medium,' which per the rules is mid-scale and cannot itself support keep_moist or any other enum value; no other admissible source frames a watering statement for this species.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength, is_edible, chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, day/night temperature fields, humidity fields, and light_fc fields are all left null: no admissible source frames Cotinus coggygria's care in these terms; this is an in-ground landscape shrub/small tree, not a houseplant, and none of the admissible pages give container-watering cadence, fertilizing schedule, chill-onset temperature, humidity range, or foot-candle light data for it.

mature_height_in/mature_spread_in use NC State's own species-page Dimensions block (10-15 ft height and width) as the anchor per the sizing rule, rather than RHS's larger 'Max Height'/'Max Spread' of 4-8 metres (about 13-26 ft) for this species; the RHS figure was not used because a species-specific NC State page exists, but the disagreement in scale between the two sources is noted here.

Missouri Botanical Garden's popup 'Common Names' list (smoketree, American smoke tree, Hungarian sumac, indian sumac, purple fringe, scotino, smoke bush, smoke tree, Turkish sumac, tyrolean sumac, Venetian sumach, venus's sumach, wig tree, young fustic, zante wood) lives only inside an onmouseover overlib attribute and was not quoted or used as evidence anywhere, per the rule against quoting that markup.

RHS's 'Other common names' field (American smoke tree, Hungarian sumac, Indian sumac, purple fringe, scotino, smoke bush, Turkish sumac, Tyrolean sumac, Venetian sumach, Venus's sumach, wig tree, young fustic, Zante wood) is a secondary field and was not used to support common_name, per the rule against drawing a primary name from an 'other common names' list.
No admissible source addressed edibility (is_edible) for Cotinus coggygria itself, so it was left null rather than inferred from the genus's culinary/dye uses mentioned elsewhere.

NC State's structured 'is often confused with:' module for this species lists Lonicera fragrantissima and Prunus cerasifera, not Cotinus obovatus; no admissible source's structured confusion module names the native American smoketree for this page, so that specific trap could not be documented from a structured field.

Six citations were repaired at landing without any value changing. Two quotes were <title> metadata presented as page content and were dropped, since rendered substitutes already support the same values: the common_name quote 'Cotinus coggygria (Common Smoketree, Smokebush, Smoketree)' and the scientific_name_accepted quote 'Cotinus coggygria | smoke tree'. Four quotes glued an NC State label to its value ('Common Name(s):', 'Problems:', 'Light:', 'Soil Texture:', 'Dimensions:', 'Attracts:') and were re-quoted as the field values the page renders. The bare one-word RHS quote 'Correct' was relabelled as the Botanical Details Name Status row and paired with two new citations that name the taxon in rendered body text: RHS's H1 and NC State's 'Cotinus coggygria is often confused with:' module heading.

normalizations: 2026-09-27: b88 landed from the post-audit records, five mixed species, alongside the b86 landing in the same tree. Phaseolus lunatus and Pastinaca sativa were researched 2026-09-11 under the 35-field schema and carry no is_edible, attracts_pollinators or mature_*_in keys; nothing was backfilled onto them. The other three were researched today under the grown schema and keep those fields where a citation carries them. Landing decisions: Phaseolus lunatus lands as Butter Beans, not the researched 'Lima Bean' — the audit FLAGGED that value because NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list puts Butter Beans first and Lima Bean third, and RHS's dedicated page leads with 'butter bean' and files 'Lima bean' under Other common names; Lima Bean is disclosed in name_note and unknowns, and the name matches the catalog's plural style for the sibling Phaseolus vulgaris (Green Beans). Pastinaca sativa's toxicity_detail was rebuilt in full — the five stacked Landscape Problems flags including Problem for Children, the four Plant Type traits, Poison Severity Medium under the human-scoped 'Poisonous to Humans:' heading, Furanocoumarin, Causes Contact Dermatitis Yes, the Poison Symptoms text with no terminal period, the complete six-part Poison Part list, NC State's furocoumarin gloves/long-sleeves warning and its 'Poisonous and causes severe dermatitis.' line, RHS's two rendered Potentially harmful lines with the HTA-guide clause restored, Clemson's rash warning, the first-year-taproot limit on edibility, the NC-State-versus-RHS disagreement on pet scope, and the poison-hemlock / cow-parsnip look-alikes — and its toxic_to_pets true rests on RHS's 'Pets (dogs): Harmful to skin with sunlight' line and NC State's Problem for Cats / Problem for Dogs flags. Its soil_ph_min/max were populated 6.5/7 on the audit's finding that RHS's species-page Cultivation paragraph states 'The ideal soil pH is 6.5-7', which the research record had missed. Parthenocissus tricuspidata takes no mature size at all under the pipeline's climber rule (NC State Plant Type: Vine, Climbing Method: Tendrils), disclosed in unknowns with the unused figures; its is_edible stays null because RHS's own page for the taxon says 'Harmful if eaten; skin irritant.' against NC State's Edible-fruit Play Value, and toxicity_detail was populated to carry both readings; toxic_to_pets stays null because RHS's 'Pets:' line names neither cats nor dogs. is_houseplant was false-and-cited on the three records that had left it null (Boston Ivy, Mugo Pine, Common Smoketree). Auditor CORRECTED WORDING was used verbatim except in Cotinus coggygria's name_note, where the parenthetical reference to 'unknowns[9]' was replaced with the substance of that entry (the overlay lives inside an onmouseover attribute and is not quoted). Twenty-seven quotes that were <title> metadata, fabricated strings, bare one-word name values, label+value splices, comma-joined runs of separately-stacked list items, or truncated or over-extended structured tag lists were replaced with rendered substitutes; every one was re-read through verify_quotes' own fetch+extract path with element boundaries made visible before it was applied, which is how two truncations the audit did not report — Pinus mugo's three-value Attracts field and its seven-value Landscape Location field — were caught. verify_quotes: every reachable quote verified; hgic.clemson.edu returns http-403 to this machine and plantfinder.mobot.org refuses the connection, so those citations SKIP.
